newsitem.title: KENYA: Tribunal accuses Rwandan mayor of sexual violence.
newsitem.headline: Tribunal accuses Rwandan mayor of sexual violence.

text.p: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda said on Wednesday its prosecutor had added sexual violence to a genocide indictment against a former Rwandan mayor.
A tribunal statement said the case of Jean Paul Akayesu would contain fresh charges of sexual violence and rape of female civilians alleged to have taken place between April and June 1994.

Akayesu has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity during the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994. He faces life imprisonment if convicted, the tribunal's highest penalty.
The tribunal said the indictment was amended on June 17 on the basis of statements from five witnesses who said women taking refuge in his commune of Taba were sexually abused.
Akayesu is the former mayor of Taba in central Rwanda.

"The amended indictment charges that Mr Akayesu knew and facilitated the commission of sexual violence, beatings and murders of mostly Tutsi women who had sought refuge at Taba bureau communal," the statement said.
"These acts of sexual violence, were generally accompanied by explicit threats of death or bodily harm," it added.

Akayesu is set to appear next on trial before the tribunal in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on September 29 charged with genocide and crimes against humanity and on October 22 for the new charges.
The tribunal also said it had granted a request for former Rwandan army colonel Theoneste Bagosora, considered the most wanted suspect already held in Arusha, to replace his lawyer.
Bagosora, who was effectively in charge of Rwanda's former Hutu army in the first few hours of the three-month mass slaughter, is also charged with genocide and crimes against humanity.

Bagosora argued he lost confidence in his defence lawyer because of an alleged lack of cooperation. The statement said the tribunal on June 27 granted his request and told the court registrar to find him another counsel.

The Rwanda tribunal, which was set up by the United Nations in 1994, has been plagued by problems in bringing to justice the leaders of the 1994 genocide sparked off by the assassination of Hutu military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana in April that year.
So far 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal, which has 12 suspects in detention in Arusha.

The Rwanda tribunal was modelled on the Hague-based criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, set up by the United Nations in 1993 and the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
